children.translated_text: Again and again, on each occasion for adding more, after blowing continuously, when the coals become thin and are covered with white ash, then charcoal should again be supplied and blowing should again be done.

children.text: evaṃ bhastrādvayena praharaparyantaṃ saṃtataṃ dhmānena prāyaḥ kaṭhinadravyāṇāṃ sattvanirgamanakālaḥ samupajāyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, by continuous blowing with two bellows up to one watch, the time for the emergence of essence from hard substances generally comes about.

children.text: paraṃ tu nāyaṃ kālaḥ sattvanirgamanajñāpakaḥ svātantreṇa kiṃtu śuklā vahnijvālaiva jñāyamānā ||
children.translated_text: But this time is not independently the indicator of the emergence of essence; rather, the white flame of the fire, when perceived, is.
For it is said in the chapter on definitions:
When the fire has blazing flames and is accompanied by a white uprising,
then one should know it as the pure turning-point; that is the time for the emergence of essence.
Thus.

children.text: tadā sphuṭipiṇḍīr bahir niṣkāsya kiṭṭaṃ pṛthakkṛtya gurumārgeṇa sattvamātraṃ grāhyam ||
children.translated_text: Then, after taking the cracked lumps out, separating the slag, one should take only the essence by the main channel.

children.text: atha dvitīyaḥ sattvapiṇḍānāṃ prakṣepakālaḥ prāpnotīti bodhyam ||
children.translated_text: Now it should be understood that the second time for adding the essence-lumps has arrived.
Now, for the falling of essence from soft substances, only slight blowing is required.
Therefore he states a special furnace useful for that, with the words 'on firm ground.'

children.text: tatra dvādaśāṅgulaṃ gartaṃ vidhāya tattalamadhye caturaṅgulagāmbhīryavistāram anyaṃ vartulaṃ gartaṃ kṛtvā garbhagartatalam ārabhya pṛṣṭhabhāgaparyantaṃ bāhyagartābhimukhaṃ tatsallagnaṃ kiṃcitsamunnataṃ tiryaṅnālasamanvitaṃ dvāraṃ vidhāya garbhagartopari mṛccakrīṃ pañcarandhraviśiṣṭāṃ vāyor ūrdhvagamanārthaṃ kṣipet ||
children.translated_text: There, after making a pit twelve fingers deep, and making another round pit in the middle of its floor, four fingers in depth and breadth, one should make, from the floor of the inner pit up to the rear side, a door facing the outer pit, joined to it, somewhat raised, and provided with a transverse tube; then above the inner pit one should place an earthen disk marked with five holes, so that the wind may go upward.

children.text: taduparyaṅgārāṃstadupari sattvapātanagolāṃśca nikṣipya sarvāṃ koṣṭhīṃ kokilaiḥ pūrayitvaikabhastrayā dhamet ||
children.translated_text: Above that one should place charcoals, and above those the balls for causing the fall of essence; after filling the whole furnace with charcoals, one should blow with a single bellows.
This is called the <s>pātālakoṣṭhikā</s> (subterranean furnace).
Having stated the furnace characterized by downward blowing, he states the furnace characterized by upward blowing with the word 'twelve.'
A furnace, a <s>prādeśa</s> in length and breadth, should be made on the surface of the ground.

children.text: sā ca talabhāgam ārabhyopari caturaṅgulabhāgaṃ vihāya tadupari valayena kaṭakena samanvitāṃ tāṃ kṛtvā valayopari prabhūtacchidrayuktāṃ cakrīṃ nikṣipya tatra kokilāṃśca dattvā vaṅkanālataḥ pradhamet ||
children.translated_text: And, beginning from the bottom part, leaving a four-finger portion above, one should make it furnished above that with a ring or band; upon the ring one should place a disk provided with many holes, put charcoals there, and blow through a bent tube.
A furnace made from a soft material mixed with a larger portion of <s>gāra</s> than clay is called a <s>gārakoṣṭhī</s>.

children.text: iyaṃ kāṃsyarītipramukhaṃ yatsṛṣṭalohaṃ tanmadhye saṃsargaghaṭakayor madhya ekasyāvaśeṣakarī dvitīyaṃ vināśyetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This means that, among produced alloys such as bronze and brass, it leaves one of the two combining constituents remaining and destroys the other.

children.text: atha siddharasānāṃ khoṭabaddhādīnām abhrakādisattvānāṃ ca kācaṭaṅkaṇasauvīrādinā śodhayituṃ sādhanabhūtāṃ koṣṭhīmāha dvādaśāṅguleti ||
children.translated_text: Now he states, with the word 'twelve fingers,' the furnace that is the instrument for purifying perfected mercuries such as those bound into pellets, and essences such as mica-essence, by means of glass, borax, sauvīra, and so on.

children.text: asyāṃ koṣṭhyāṃ sthāpitamūṣāmadhye siddharasādi prakṣipya saṃtatadhmānāvasare 'ntarāntarā muhuḥ kācacūrṇādi dattvā dhamet ||
children.translated_text: In this furnace, after placing the prepared mercury and the like inside a crucible set there, one should blow continuously, and at intervals repeatedly add powdered glass and the like while blowing.
'Soft substance' means essence and the like.

children.text: iyaṃ koṣṭhī budhnabhāgamārabhya mukhabhāgaparyantaṃ kramavistṛtā prādeśapramitavartulamukhī kāryetyanuktamapi bodhyam ||
children.translated_text: Although not explicitly stated, it should be understood that this furnace is to be made gradually wider from the bottom part up to the mouth, with a round mouth measuring a <s>prādeśa</s>.
For the former one was stated to have a mouth of that same measure.

children.text: saṃprati mūṣākoṣṭhyapekṣyādhikatarāgnijanakapuṭān vaktuṃ teṣāṃ prayojanamāha raseti ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to speak of puṭa-firings that generate more abundant fire than a crucible-furnace requires, he states their purpose with the word 'mercury.'
For hard substances such as mercury and metals, complete cooking is required for medicinal use.

children.text: sa ca pākaḥ kriyārūpastulayā parimāṇena vā paricchettuṃ na śakyate ||
children.translated_text: And that cooking, being an operation, cannot be delimited by a scale or by a measure.
Only a puṭa, that is, a particular pit filled with fire-kindling stones, husks, cow-dung cakes, and so on, can serve as the means of knowing the measure of proper cooking.
When one proper cooking has been accomplished by the fire from cow-dung cakes filling such a pit, the repetition of that particular puṭa should be performed.
The intention is: until the acquisition of the qualities stated.
With insufficient cooking, smell, color, taste, and touch do not arise properly.

children.text: adhipākena tu dravyaṃ niḥsāraṃ dagdhaṃ bhavatyodanavat ||
children.translated_text: But with excessive cooking the substance becomes sapless and burnt, like cooked rice.

children.text: atha puṭasya yogato guṇāṃllohasthān āha lohāderiti ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the qualities present in metals through the application of puṭa, with the phrase 'of metal and so on.'
'Non-reversion' means not being reduced to the natural state, even by the treatment with the five friends.

children.text: guṇādhikyamāmāvasthāpanne tasmin bhakṣite jāṭharāgnyapākena rogavārakā guṇāstathā puṣṭyādayo mārdavādayaścānudbhūtāsteṣām udbhavenādhikyābhāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The increase of qualities is an apparent superiority through the manifestation of qualities which, when it was in the raw state and had been eaten, had not arisen because the digestive fire had not cooked it: qualities that prevent disease, as well as nourishment and the like, softness and the like.
By that comes excellence: superiority and greater value.

children.text: tathāpsu prakṣiptasya tasya na majjanam uparitaraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, when it is thrown into water, it does not sink but floats on the surface.

children.text: aṅgulibhyāṃ pīḍitasya tasya sūkṣmāṅgulirekhāsu praviṣṭatvaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: And when pressed by the fingers, it enters into the fine lines of the fingers.
But in special stones such as mica, diamond, and orpiment, qualities such as lightness appear from puṭa-firing.
What is the use of saying much in praise of the qualities?

children.text: yatra guṇāḥ sarve sambhūyotkaṭā nivasanti tasmāt pāradādapi jīrṇarasoparasamaṇilohāt susiddhānāṃ lohānāṃ guṇā yathāvidhisevino narasya śarīre'dhikā eva ||
children.translated_text: Where all qualities dwell together in an intense form, therefore, even more than from mercury, the qualities of well-prepared metals, digested mineral essences, secondary minerals, jewels, and metals are greater in the body of a man who uses them according to rule.

children.text: bhūriphalayuto'pi siddharasasya hi krāmaṇārthaṃ kiṃcitsphuṭitayauvanā kāminī saṃnihitāpekṣyate bhāṣaṇacumbanāliṅganārthaṃ tatstanābhyāmaṅgamardanārthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: For even though perfected mercury has abundant effects, for its penetration a woman with somewhat blossoming youth must be nearby for conversation, kissing, and embracing, and for massaging the body with her breasts.
In her absence, because there is no penetration through the whole body, <s>Manmatha</s> does not arise.
But in her presence, through carelessness, sexual intercourse may occur.
And from that death may result.
Moreover, for one who uses mercury there are special restrictions lasting for a year.
At the beginning, the preparation of the body-field is also necessary.
For the perfection of mercury, one requires someone capable of carrying out all the procedures known by experience, and also abundant wealth and other resources.

children.text: ata eva nātinirapāyasya lohasya guṇānām ādhikyamupacaryate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, precisely for this reason, the greater qualities of metal, which is not very dangerous, are spoken of figuratively as superior.

children.text: nanu pāṣāṇato'pi kaṭhināṇāṃ lohaviśeṣāṇāṃ nāvayavaviśleṣa iti katham uktalābha ityāśaṅkya nidarśanena punarlohaguṇān dṛḍhīkaroti yathāśmanīti ||
children.translated_text: But one may object: since there is no separation of the parts of particular metals, which are harder even than stone, how can the obtaining just mentioned occur? Anticipating this, he again confirms the properties of metals by an example, with the words "as in stone."
The sense is that everything becomes possible through the entrance of the internal fire.

children.text: saṃprati gartāviśeṣaṃ mahāpuṭamāha bhūmimadhya iṣṭikādibhiḥ kṛte kuḍye kuḍyamaye garte gāmbhīryavistārābhyāṃ dvihaste tathā catuṣkoṇe tādṛggarte vanyacchagaṇaiḥ sahasrasaṃkhyākaiḥ pūrite sati śarāvasaṃpuṭitaṃ bheṣajaṃ piṣṭikopari pūritacchagaṇopari sthāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Now he describes a particular pit, the <s>mahāpuṭa</s>. In the middle of the ground, in a walled pit made with bricks and the like, a pit made of walls, two cubits in depth and breadth and likewise square, when such a pit has been filled with one thousand forest cow-dung cakes, the medicine enclosed in a pair of earthen saucers should be placed on top of the paste, above the filled dung-cakes.
Above such a crucible one should fill in half a thousand dung-cakes.
Then one should ignite it.
Next he describes the <s>gajapuṭa</s>, with the words "a royal cubit."
A royal cubit measures thirty fingers.

children.text: tanmitaṃ nimnaṃ gambhīraṃ tanmitavistāraṃ ca gartaṃ bodhyaṃ ||
children.translated_text: One should understand that the pit is deep, having a depth of that measure, and also a breadth of that measure.
In the word "deep," the word "breadth" is indicated elliptically.
One should fill it up to the neck with those stone-like dung-cakes.
The <s>upalas</s> are hard, large forest dung-cakes; the <s>śāṭhīs</s> are smaller-bodied ones than those.

children.text: tatra mūṣāṃ bheṣajagarbhitāṃ vinyasya pūrvavinyastacchagaṇato'rdhamānāni giriṇḍāni vanyacchagaṇāni vinikṣipet ityetadgajapuṭākhyaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: Placing there a crucible containing the medicine, one should throw in compact lumps, forest dung-cakes, measuring half as much as the dung-cakes previously placed. This is considered the method called <s>gajapuṭa</s>.
Next he describes the <s>kukkuṭapuṭa</s>.

children.text: bhūmipṛṣṭhabhāge kuḍyena nirmitaṃ caturviṃśatyaṅgulocchrāyaṃ tāvanmānameva tale mukhe ca vistṛtametādṛśaṃ yadgartaṃ bheṣajaṃ paktumupalādibhiḥ pūryate tatkukkuṭapuṭasaṃjñaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: A pit constructed with a wall on the surface of the ground, twenty-four fingers high and just as broad at the bottom and at the mouth, which is filled with dung-cakes and the like for cooking medicine, is called <s>kukkuṭapuṭa</s>.

children.text: yacca gartaṃ bhūmitale mṛdādibhiḥ kṛtamaṣṭasaṃkhyairvanopalairdīyate jvālayā prajvalitaṃ kriyate baddhapāradasya bhasmakaraṇārthaṃ tatkapotapuṭamucyate ||
children.translated_text: And the pit that is made on the ground with clay and the like, and is fired, made blazing with flame, by eight forest dung-cakes for the purpose of making ash from bound mercury, is called <s>kapotapuṭa</s>.

children.text: gorvaraistuṣairvā yatra gajapuṭagartāyāṃ puṭaṃ dīyate bheṣajaṃ pakvaṃ kriyate tadgorvarapuṭamucyate ||
children.translated_text: Where a puṭa is applied in a <s>gajapuṭa</s> pit with cow-dung cakes or husks, and the medicine is cooked, that is called <s>gorvarapuṭa</s>.
Next he describes the <s>bhūdharapuṭa</s>, with the word "fire-friend."
The fire-friend is a crucible, that is to say, an earthen saucer.
Its use should be understood in procedures for <s>jayasundara</s> and other mercury preparations.
Next he describes the <s>lāvakapuṭa</s>, with the word "above."

children.text: śarāvākāramūṣāṃ saṃpuṭitāṃ bhūmau nidhāya tadupari ṣoḍaśavanopalamitais tuṣair gorvarair vā yatpuṭaṃ dīyate pākaḥ kriyate tallāvakam iti khyātam ||
children.translated_text: Having placed in the ground a lidded crucible shaped like an earthen saucer, the puṭa that is applied over it with husks or cow-dung cakes equal to sixteen forest dung-cakes, and by which cooking is performed, is known as <s>lāvaka</s>.
The number sixteen itself is called <s>ṣoḍaśikā</s>.
And here that number is to be taken only with respect to the forest dung-cakes.
The meaning is: with that much, that is, with an amount equal to those forest goat-dung cakes.
For, since puṭas are generally accomplished by forest dung-cakes, their presence is implied.
Now I shall state the <s>kumbhapuṭa</s>, as taught in another text.
In an earthen pot, having made many holes, each equal to a finger,
forty in number, then in it one should place cool powdered charcoal.
After filling it halfway, one should put an earthen saucer over the mouth.

children.text: karpaṭena mṛdā liptvā chāyāśuṣkaṃ ca kārayet ||
children.translated_text: Having smeared it with cloth and clay, one should cause it to dry in the shade.

children.text: tasminnaṅgārakān kṣiptvā cullyāṃ vā ceṣṭikāsu ca
children.translated_text: Having put coals into it, and having placed it on a stove or among bricks,
when it is cool after three days, one should take it and remove the medicine.
This should be known as the <s>kumbhapuṭa</s>, as declared by those who know the śāstra.
Thus.
He states the purifying group and its use, with the words "with glass, borax, and sauvīra."
<s>Sauvīra</s> is a particular kind of collyrium.

children.text: ayaṃ gaṇaḥ sūtasya khoṭabaddhādirūpasyābhrakasattvādīnāṃ ca yo guṇo vaṅgakāpālikā nāgakāpālikā kālikādir doṣātmakastaddhvaṃsī ||
children.translated_text: This group destroys the defect that is of the nature of tin-cupellation, lead-cupellation, blackening, and the like, which is a property of mercury in such forms as a bound pellet, and also of mica-essence and the like.
For this very reason it is approved by practitioners of mercury science.
With the word "poison" he proceeds.
These defects are natural.
Because the removal of separation from them is extremely difficult in comparison with other defects, they are figuratively called innate.

children.text: vastutastu devaprārthitamahādevena teṣāṃ saṃbandhaḥ pārade yojita iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But in reality, the sense is that their connection with mercury was established by <s>Mahādeva</s>, who had been entreated by the gods.
He states the two compounded defects with the word "yaugika."

children.text: nikaṭavartināgavaṅgakhaniyogena miśraṇājjāto nāgākhya eko doṣo vaṅgākhya ekaśceti tau dvau jāḍyamādhmānaṃ kuṣṭhaṃ ca kurutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Through mixture caused by the connection of nearby lead and tin mines, one defect called lead-born and another called tin-born arise; these two produce dullness, swelling, and skin disease.

children.text: upādhinā saṃnihitavastusaṃbandhamātreṇa vastuni bahireva vyāpya tiṣṭhanti kiṃcit kālāvasthāyinaśca ye doṣāste aupādhikāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those defects which, through an adjunct, merely by connection with a nearby substance, pervade and remain externally in the substance, and which last for some time, are adventitious.
And these are of seven kinds.
They are stated in the śāstra under the name <s>kañcuka</s>.
Among them, those born from the earth are of one type.
Because their minor subdivisions have no use in the śāstra, the plural is used without regard to naming them individually.
Those born from mountains are of one kind.
Those born from water, aquatic ones, are another kind.

children.text: tathā nāgena vaṇijādibhir miśrīkṛtena jātau doṣau dvau ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, there are two defects produced by lead mixed in by merchants and others.
And there are also two produced from tin.

children.text: ityevaṃ sapta kañcukāḥ pūrvoktāśca pañca doṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus there are seven <s>kañcukas</s>, together with the five defects mentioned before.

children.text: itthaṃ pārade dvādaśa doṣā rasajñaiḥ proktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this way twelve defects in mercury are declared by those who know mercury science.
He gives other names for the seven <s>kañcukas</s> just mentioned, in order, with the word "parpaṭī."
On the surface of mercury there is <s>parpaṭī</s>, having the form of a thin flake.
That is called <s>parpaṭī</s>.
<s>Pāṭanī</s> is that which causes splitting of the skin.
<s>Bhedī</s> is that which makes holes in the skin.
Drāvī means that which liquefies metals and the like.
Malakarī means that which produces impurity and disorders such as vāta.
Andhakārī means that which produces blackness.
Dhvāṅkṣī means blackness.

children.text: atha prathamādhyāye mūrchitvā harati rujam itipadyoktā viṣayāstraya evātra granthe vaktavyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, the three topics mentioned in the verse in the first chapter, "having been stupefied, it removes disease," are precisely the ones to be explained in this work.
They are mūrchana (stupefaction), bandhana (binding), and māraṇa (killing or calcination).

children.text: tatra mūrchanaṃ tu mardanapūrvakaṃ puṭena prāguktameva ||
children.translated_text: Among these, mūrchana preceded by grinding and done with a puṭa (sealed heating) has already been stated before.
But in this chapter I shall explain mechanical mūrchana after all bindings useful for the body.
The second topic here is described in the form of bandha (binding).
The phrase "twenty-five" means this.
Now, in another work, bandha is taught as only fourfold: pāṭa, khoṭa, jalūkā, and bhasman.
But here he declares that it is numbered as twenty-five.

children.text: etadviruddhamiva bhātītyāśaṅkya cāñcalyadurgrahatvābhāvarūpasāmānyasya sarvabandheṣu sattve'pi bandhajanakakāraṇabhedānurodhena bandhabhedo'pi vārtikairādṛta ityāha yena yeneti ||
children.translated_text: Anticipating the objection, "This seems contradictory," he says, with "by whichever," that although the general property consisting in absence of mobility and difficulty of grasping exists in all bindings, the authorities on vārtika accept distinctions among bindings according to distinctions among the causes that produce binding.

children.text: pāradam āpaṇād ānīya nimbūrasena saṃmardya gālayitvā mayūratutthādisamabhāgaṃ caturthāṃśaṃ vā tatra dattvā mardanena baddho rasaḥ kriyate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury is brought from the market, ground with lemon juice, filtered, and then an equal portion, or a fourth part, of peacock-blue vitriol and the like is added to it; by grinding, bound mercury is made.
If that is consumed, it may cause death or disease.
He states the definition of āroṭa with "well purified."

children.text: trividhapātanena śuddhaṃ paścācchuddhaṃ cūrṇīkṛtam abhrakadalaṃ samabhāgaṃ dattvā kāñjikena mardanapūrvakaṃ pāradaṃ naṣṭapiṣṭaṃ kṛtvordhvādhastiryakpātanenāsakṛtkṛtenāgnisahaḥ pārada āroṭa iti nigadyate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury purified by the threefold distillation, then with an equal portion of purified powdered mica sheets added, ground with sour gruel until it has become a lost paste, and made able to withstand fire by repeated upward, downward, and transverse distillation, is called āroṭa.

children.text: taṃ ca mākṣīkaśilājatulohacūrṇapathyākṣaviḍaṅgaghṛtamadhubhiḥ saṃyutaṃ kṛtvā kṣetrīkaraṇāya yuñjīteti rasahṛdaye ||
children.translated_text: And in the <s>Rasahṛdaya</s> it is said that one should use that, combined with pyrite, bitumen, iron powder, chebulic myrobalan, marking-nut, false black pepper, ghee, and honey, for preparing the field of the body.

children.text: mākṣīkasahito naṣṭapiṣṭirūpaḥ pātanenāgnisthāyyapi pārado'pi āroṭa iti kathyate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury in the form of a lost paste, combined with pyrite and, though subjected to distillation, remaining stable in fire, is also called āroṭa.

children.text: ābhāsalakṣaṇamāha yaḥ pārado dhātubhir manaḥśilāgandhakādibhistathā mūlikādyaiḥ sarpākṣyādimūlikābhiḥ patrapuṣpādibhiśca saha bhāvito dravaṃ dattvā marditastato bhūdharayantre puṭena puṭito bhasmīkṛtaḥ svabhāvataḥ svabhāvaṃ cāñcalyadurgrahatvādi muktvā dhātvādiyogaṃ yāti tattadroganāśakayogaguṇaṃ ca yāti guṇaprado bhavati ||
children.translated_text: He states the definition of ābhāsa: mercury that has been treated with metals, with realgar, sulphur, and the like, and likewise with herbs such as sarpākṣī and other plants, with leaves, flowers, and so on, has been ground after adding liquid, then heated in a puṭa in a bhūdhara apparatus and reduced to ash, and naturally, abandoning its nature such as mobility and difficulty of grasping, enters into combination with metals and the like, and also acquires the properties of the respective disease-destroying compound, becoming a giver of benefits.

children.text: alpakālaparyantaṃ tataḥ pathyasevino'pi narasya guṇavaikṛte sati guṇavikriyāyāṃ satyāṃ sa baddhapārada ābhāsa iti kīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For only a short time, when a person who follows the regimen experiences alteration of the qualities, that is, transformation of the qualities, that bound mercury is called ābhāsa.
Because it produces only an appearance of qualities.
Vaikṛta is simply vikṛti, alteration.
The phrase "conch and oyster-shell" means this.

children.text: bhasmīkṛtānāṃ śaṅkhaśuktyādīnāṃ vṛkṣakṣārādīnāṃ ca mūṣāṃ kṛtvā tatsaṃpuṭe pāradaṃ prakṣipya saṃpuṭitaḥ pārado laghupuṭadānena bhasmībhavatīti kṣārabandho 'sāvagnidīptyādikṛd bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Having made a crucible from calcined conch, oyster-shell, and the like, and also from plant alkalis and the like, one should place mercury in that enclosure; the mercury, enclosed, becomes ash by the application of a light puṭa. This is kṣārabandha, and it may produce kindling of the digestive fire and the like.
Now he states khoṭabandha with "binding."
As for the method of making khoṭa, the <s>Rasasāra</s> says:
The eight great medicines that are well known in binding
should be used, combined with borax, to impregnate the lord of mercury.
By blowing it in a crucible smeared with them, it becomes khoṭa.
Thus.
That same substance is destroyed by excessive blowing.
And that should be understood as khoṭabandha.
Here mercury in which sulphur six times its quantity has been digested should be taken.
Or one made into a paste by the addition of mica should be taken.
Having ground it in the juice of somavallī, one should give it three puṭas,
and should impregnate it seven times with the juice of somavallī itself.

children.text: tadabhraṃ mṛdbhāṇḍe dadyād rasena saha saṃyutam
children.translated_text: That mica should be placed in an earthen vessel together with mercury.
The root of śarapuṅkhā should be rubbed with cow's milk.

children.text: kalkena melayet sūtaṃ gaganaṃ ca tadadhordhvagam
children.translated_text: One should mix the mercury and the mica that moves above and below with that paste.

children.text: sthāpayed ravitāpe tu nirmukho grasate kṣaṇāt
children.translated_text: One should place it in the heat of the sun; without opening, it swallows it in a moment.

children.text: jāyate piṣṭikā śīghraṃ nātra kāryā vicāraṇā ||
children.translated_text: A paste is quickly produced; no doubt need be entertained here.
Thus.

children.text: piṣṭībandhastu khoṭaka iti varṇanād atra piṣṭikārūpam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Since piṣṭībandha is described as khoṭaka, here its paste-form is being stated.
But in another work the definition of khoṭa is:

children.text: dhmāto druto bhavet khoṭa āhataścūrṇatāṃ vrajet
children.translated_text: When blown, it becomes melted; when struck, it becomes powder.

children.text: punar dhmāto drutaḥ khoṭa iti khoṭasya lakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: When blown again, it melts: this is the definition of khoṭa.

children.text: ghanasattvapādajīrṇaḥ kāntapādajīrṇaḥ samatīkṣṇajīrṇaścedvāyaṃ kṣetrīkaraṇārtham api praśastaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If this has digested one quarter of the essence of mica, one quarter of magnetite, or an equal amount of sharp iron, it is also excellent for preparing the field of the body.
He defines pāṭabandha with "melted."

children.text: adho'gninā kaṭāhe tāpena drutā jātadravā yā kajjalī sā tatkṣaṇe kadalīdale prakṣipya taddalenācchādya pīḍanena cipiṭīkṛtā pāṭabandhaḥ parpaṭikābandhaśceti khyātā bālavṛddhādīnām anupānabhedena sarvarogaghnī ||
children.translated_text: Kajjalī that has been melted, becoming liquid by the heat of a cauldron with fire below, is immediately placed on a plantain leaf, covered with that leaf, and flattened by pressing; this is known as pāṭabandha and parpaṭikābandha, and according to differences in the vehicle it destroys all diseases of children, the elderly, and others.
He defines kajjalībandha.
When kajjalī is furnished, through the respective compound, with the process of mixing and grinding with special disease-preventing medicines, it is called kajjalībandha.
Here the statement "combined with the respective compound" is not a constituent of the definition.
Because kajjalī is accomplished even without that.
Rather, that statement is made to convey that, because it acts as a yogavāhin (catalytic carrier), it destroys all diseases.
He explains sajīvabaddha with the words "made into ash."

children.text: tāmbūlīdalarasamarditaḥ paścād vandhyākarkoṭakīkandamadhye prakṣipya saṃpuṭito bahir mṛdvastrābhyāṃ saṃpuṭito bhūmau gajapuṭena puṭito bhasmībhavati ||
children.translated_text: After being ground with the juice of betel leaves, it is then put inside the tuber of sterile karkoṭakī, sealed in a covered vessel, enclosed outside with clay and cloth, and heated in the earth with a gajapuṭa; it becomes ash.

children.text: evaṃ prakārāntareṇāpi bhasmīkṛtaḥ pārado'gnau pātre dhṛtaścedākāśe gacchati ||
children.translated_text: Mercury made into ash in this way, or also by another method, if held in a vessel over fire, goes into the sky.
Because its wings have not been cut off.

children.text: bhasmakāryaṃ jarāmaraṇābhāvarūpaṃ sa tu na karoti ||
children.translated_text: But it does not perform the function of ash, namely the absence of old age and death.
Nor does it destroy disease.
He characterizes nirbījabandha with the words "but mercury."

children.text: atra suvarṇaṃ na tu bījīkṛtaṃ kiṃtu śuddhaṃ jāraṇāyantre saṃskṛtaṃ pattrarūpaṃ grāhyam ||
children.translated_text: Here gold should not be taken as one that has been made into a seed, but as pure gold, processed in a jāraṇa apparatus and in leaf form.

children.text: piṣṭīkṛto dvādaśāṃśe pārada ekāṃśaṃ gandhakaṃ truṭiśo muhur dattvāmlena saṃmarditastatastulyāṃśagandhaiḥ krameṇa puṭitaḥ prathamaṃ gandhakaṃ caturthāṃśaṃ dattvā bhūdharayantre puṭitastato'rdhāṃśaṃ gandhakaṃ dattvā tathā puṭitastataḥ pādonaṃ gandhakaṃ dattvā puṭitastadūrdhvaṃ samabhāgamitaṃ dattvā puṭita iti kramaśabdārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When mercury has been made into a paste, one twelfth part sulphur should be added to one part little by little and repeatedly, and it should be ground with acid. Then it is heated in puṭas successively with equal parts of sulphurs: first a fourth part sulphur is added and it is heated in a bhūdhara apparatus; then half as much sulphur is added and it is heated in the same way; then sulphur deficient by a quarter is added and it is heated; after that an equal quantity is added and it is heated. This is the meaning of the word "successively."
The plural in "with sulphurs" is not significant.

children.text: vajreṇa bhasmīkṛtena cūrṇīkṛtena vā nihato mārito yaḥ sūtastanmadhye māritam anyaṃ sūtakam api nikṣipet ||
children.translated_text: Mercury that has been struck down, that is, killed, by calcined or powdered diamond: into that one should also put another killed mercury.

children.text: so'pi raso baddhaḥ khoṭarūpaḥ śṛṅkhalābaddha ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: That mercury too, bound in the form of a khoṭa, is called śṛṅkhalābaddha, "chain-bound."
This method of killing is stated in the <s>Rasārṇava</s>.
Now he explains drutibaddha with the words "though joined."

children.text: bījānāṃ jāraṇena yadi raso mahāprabhāvo bhavatīti tanna citram ||
children.translated_text: If mercury becomes very powerful through the digestion of seeds, that is no wonder.

children.text: rasoparasadhātūnāṃ yā bahirdrutayas tābhir yukto'pi tābhir jārito'pi pārado baddhamātro bandhottaraṃ bhasmīkṛto vā drutibaddhanāmā sarṣapacaturthāṃśamātrayā sevitaścedduḥsādhyarogān nihanti ||
children.translated_text: Mercury, even when joined with the external drutis of minerals, secondary minerals, and metals, and even when digested with them, if merely bound, or made into ash after binding, is named drutibaddha; when consumed in a dose of only a quarter of a mustard seed, it destroys diseases difficult to cure.
He characterizes the binding called bāla with "together."
Abhra means the essence of black vajrābhra mica.
Śivaja means mercury.
Digested with an equal quantity of mica means according to a sequence of parts such as sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, and so on.
Its use should also be understood in coating leaves.
He characterizes mūrtibaddha with "which."
The divine herbs are the sixty-four herbs mentioned earlier; through their juice, by grinding, steaming, and the like, there is cutting off of the wings.

children.text: abhrajāraṇād vināpyatyagnisaho baddhaḥ kṛto dravyāntarānabhivyāptyā kevalaṃ dehenaiva baddho mūrtibaddha ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Even without digestion of mica, mercury that has been made able to withstand very intense fire and bound without pervasion by another substance, bound only by its own body, is called mūrtibaddha.
Likewise, through contact with vaikrānta and diamond.

children.text: tena cūrṇīkṛtena saha mardanādapi raso baddho bhavatīti so'pi mūrtibaddha ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury also becomes bound by grinding it together with that when powdered, and that too is called mūrtibaddha.
Thus mūrtibandha can be of two kinds.
He characterizes jalabandha.

children.text: śilātoyamukhaiḥ śilātoyacandratoyapramukhair jalaiḥ saha mardanādinā baddhaḥ pārado jalabaddha iti kīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Mercury bound by grinding and the like with waters such as śilā-water, candra-water, and others beginning with śilā-water is called jalabaddha.
"Stated in the kalpa" means this.
The meaning is: having the result stated in the Pāradakalpa.
The detailed account of this water is made clear in the <s>Rasārṇava</s>.

children.text: kṣiptaṃ jale bhavet kāṣṭhaṃ śilābhūtaṃ ca dṛśyate
children.translated_text: Wood thrown into the water becomes stone-like and is seen to be so;
outside and inside, O goddess, that is proclaimed to be a penetrant.

children.text: hiṅgulaṃ haritālaṃ ca gandhakaṃ ca manaḥśilā
children.translated_text: Hiṅgula, haritāla, sulphur, and manaḥśilā:

children.text: eṣāṃ gandhāpahāraṃ yat kurute tacca vedhakam ||
children.translated_text: that which removes the smell of these is also a penetrant.
Now he explains fire-bound mercury with "alone."

children.text: ādau ṣaḍguṇenābhrakajāraṇenāgnisahaḥ pārado maṇijīrṇaḥ pātanāyantreṇotthāpitaḥ sa druto bhavati ||
children.translated_text: First, mercury made able to withstand fire by digestion with six times its quantity of mica, digested with gems and raised by a distillation apparatus, becomes liquid.

children.text: sa ca kevalastīkṣṇalohayukto vā dhmātaḥ san guṭikākṛtiścāgnāvakṣayaśca bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And that, either alone or combined with sharp iron, when blown, becomes pill-shaped and does not waste away in fire.
For this very reason it is called agnibaddha, fire-bound.
If this is held in the mouth, it may give a man the power of moving through the sky, invulnerability to weapons and fire, and liberation such as sāyujya and sārūpya.
He explains mahābandha with "with gold or."

children.text: atra hema caturthāṃśam ardhāṃśaṃ vā grāhyam ||
children.translated_text: Here gold should be taken as one fourth part or one half part.
Silver likewise.

children.text: bandhauṣadhiliptavajramūṣāmadhye tayor anyatareṇa yukto dhmāto'gnibaddha eva pārado vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇaviśiṣṭaḥ susaṃskṛtakṛtasaṃjñāṃ mahābandhasaṃjñāṃ ca labhate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury that is fire-bound, combined with either of those two inside a diamond crucible smeared with binding herbs and blown, and distinguished by the characteristics to be stated, receives the name susaṃskṛtakṛt and also the name mahābandha.

children.text: tānyeva lakṣaṇāny āha dhmāto vrajatyekatām ityādinā ||
children.translated_text: He states those very characteristics with "when blown it goes into unity" and so on.
Like cloth.
It reaches a powdered state like rock salt.
When struck, it melts.
The remainder is "through contact with fire."
He explains parpaṭī mercury with "mercury, twice as much."

children.text: sabhṛṅgakaṃ bhṛṅgarājarasena mardayitvā taptaṃ drāvitaṃ tadgomayoparisthe kadale snigdhayā lohadarvyā prakṣipya tadupari kadalīdale nyubje gomayaṃ dattvā karatalādinā nipīḍya parpaṭākāraṃ kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: After grinding it with bhṛṅgarāja juice, together with bhṛṅga, one should heat and melt it, pour it with a greased iron ladle onto a plantain leaf placed over cow-dung, then put an inverted plantain leaf over it, place cow-dung on top, and press it with the palm or the like to make it into the shape of a thin parpaṭā cake.

children.text: kadalīdalasthāne snigdhe lohapatre vinikṣiptā cellohaparpaṭikā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: If it is placed on a greased iron plate instead of a plantain leaf, it becomes iron parpaṭikā.

children.text: athavā tāmrapatre snigdhe vinikṣiptā tāmraparpaṭikā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Or, if it is placed on a greased copper plate, it becomes copper parpaṭikā.
But over the mercury, a plantain leaf or the like should indeed be placed.
